title: Children's questions
hook: answer children's questions honestly, including "I don't know"
tomorrow: Gurveer's tying his first full turban. why call cloth a crown?

segments.voice: Last week ended in the kirtan room, a teacher clapping until Fateh found the beat: small voices sing. This week, the small voice has questions.

Bebe Jaswant's kitchen, Monday, after school. Chilies from her garden are drying on a tray by the window. Fateh is eating a paratha and drawing a dinosaur, and Simran is meant to be doing calculus. Then, mouth full, he asks it. When did God make the world? Before the dinosaurs or after? Simran opens her mouth. She knows something about the dinosaurs. She knows nothing at all about the other half of that question, and she can feel herself about to make something up. Bebe, at the stove, doesn't turn around. She says three words.
screen: `BEBE'S KITCHEN, AFTER SCHOOL.` → `"WHEN DID GOD MAKE THE WORLD?"` → `ABOUT TO MAKE SOMETHING UP.` → `BEBE SAYS THREE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Bebe says: nobody knows that. Then she turns around, spoon in hand, and says Guru Nanak asked the same question, and didn't pretend either. It's in Japji, the morning prayer, pauri twenty-one, on ang 4. In paraphrase: what was that time, that moment, that day, that season, when the world was made? The pandits didn't find it, or it would be written in their Puranas. The qazis didn't find it, or it would be written in their books. The yogi doesn't know it. Only the Creator who made the world knows. Look at what Guru Nanak does there. He names the learned people of both neighbors around him, and he doesn't mock them. He just says honestly: they don't know, and neither does any of us. The answer to the hardest question in the room is, I don't know. Then Bebe does the second half, which matters just as much. She tells Fateh what she does know. That the Granth opens with one Creator. That the world was made by the Hukam, the Order. And that the dinosaurs came long before people did, which his science book can tell him more about than she can. Fateh nods, satisfied, and goes back to his dinosaur. An honest I don't know didn't scare him. It made the true parts easier to trust.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS THAT.` · `JAPJI 21: WHAT WAS THAT TIME?` · `ONLY THE CREATOR KNOWS.` · `THEN SAY WHAT YOU DO KNOW.` · then, large: `HONEST ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring up one question you can't answer: about God, about your life, about someone you love. Don't try to solve it. Let it sit there honestly unanswered, and notice what you do know around its edges.
Children's questions. Answered honestly, with I don't know where it's true, and what you do know next to it.
Your line: honest answers. For the dinner table: nobody knows that, but here's what I do know. Good night.

screen: `DAY 1646 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 20 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: A FIRST FULL TURBAN. WHY CALL CLOTH A CROWN?`

howItsDone: Sikh parents and grandparents answer children's questions about God from Gurbani where they can, and Japji's twenty-first pauri gives them words for saying honestly that some things only the Creator knows.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Jap, the name of Guru Nanak's morning prayer, often called Japji.

what a scholar hears: Japji's twenty-first pauri on ang 4: neither the pandits' Puranas nor the qazis' books record the moment of creation; only the Creator knows.

chat.says: now he wants to know where his goldfish went when it died. bebe's at the gurdwara. help 😬
options: say what you don't know, then what you do: you loved it, and it's okay to miss it.
tell him it's swimming in heaven now, so he stops being sad tonight.
tell him he's too young for death questions, and change the subject.
chat.meaning: Bebe's way: an honest I don't know, then the true things you're sure of. A made-up answer is easy tonight and hard to take back later.

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's morning prayer, which opens the Granth

Puranas.meaning: ancient Hindu books of stories and lore

qazis.meaning: Muslim judges and scholars of law
